market_context: United States; FDA agricultural biotechnology and USDA bioengineered-food disclosure terminology
title: Genetically Modified Foods: What They Actually Are

seo.title: Genetically Modified Foods: What Are GMOs?
seo.meta_description: GMO is the common term for foods made from organisms whose DNA was changed using genetic engineering. U.S. labels may instead use the narrower statutory term “bioengineered,” which depends partly on detectable modified genetic material.
seo.search_intent: Explain what genetically modified foods are, how the U.S. bioengineered label relates to GMO, and what GMO status does not say about nutrition.

excerpt: “GMO” is the common consumer term for organisms whose DNA has been changed using genetic engineering. In U.S. labeling, “bioengineered” is a specific federal disclosure term with a narrower definition, so GMO and a mandatory BE disclosure are related but not identical concepts.
content_html:
The letters GMO describe a method of changing an organism, not a single ingredient or nutrition profile. FDA uses GMO as the common consumer term for plants, animals, or microorganisms whose DNA has been changed using genetic engineering, including targeted changes that conventional breeding would not make in the same way.

Genetic engineering changes specific genetic material

Traditional breeding mixes genetic traits through reproduction and selection. Genetic engineering can make more targeted changes, including introducing or altering specific DNA. Crops have been engineered for traits such as insect resistance, herbicide tolerance, storage characteristics, or altered composition.

“Bioengineered” is the U.S. disclosure term

The USDA National Bioengineered Food Disclosure Standard defines a bioengineered food as one containing detectable genetic material modified through specified in-vitro recombinant-DNA techniques when the modification could not otherwise be obtained through conventional breeding or found in nature.

Because detectability is part of that disclosure definition, a highly refined ingredient derived from a bioengineered crop may not require the same disclosure if modified genetic material is no longer detectable. That does not rewrite the crop’s production history; it reflects the scope of the labeling law.

GMO status is not a nutrition score

Genetic engineering can be used for many different traits, so the letters GMO do not tell you whether a food is high in protein, low in sugar, or rich in fiber. FDA says foods from genetically engineered plants on the U.S. market are held to the same food-safety requirements as foods from traditionally bred plants and, as a class, do not present different or greater safety concerns.

The label answers a production question

If you want to know about bioengineered status, use the applicable disclosure and ingredient information. If you want to compare calories, sodium, fiber, or added sugar, use the Nutrition Facts panel instead.

Think of GMO as a description of biotechnology used to develop an organism; it is not a shorthand verdict on the finished food’s nutritional quality.

faq.question: What does GMO mean?
faq.answer: It is the common term for an organism whose genetic material has been changed using genetic engineering.

faq.question: Is bioengineered the same as GMO on U.S. labels?
faq.answer: They overlap, but “bioengineered” has a specific federal disclosure definition that includes detectable modified genetic material, so it is not a perfect synonym in every labeling situation.

faq.question: Does GMO status tell me whether a food is healthy?
faq.answer: No. It describes how an organism was developed; nutrition depends on the specific food and its composition.
